caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Rwanda's debt has risen steadily as the government borrowed to fund its development model, but from a low base and with strong institutions. From 18.5% of GDP in 2008, the series low, the ratio climbed through the 2010s on infrastructure and the Bugesera airport project: 66.7% in 2020, the series high, after COVID borrowing, easing only slightly to a projected 64.9% in 2025. Rwanda borrows concessionally and on Eurobond markets, and IMF assessments judge the risk of distress moderate, the best in the region. The question is whether the high-investment model generates the returns to service the debt; so far growth has been strong enough to keep the ratio stable, but the margin is narrowing.
inflation_management: Rwanda's inflation has been moderate with two major spikes. It hit 15.4% in 2008, the series high, on the global food-fuel crisis, then settled into a 1-6% range for a decade as the central bank's monetary framework matured. The 2022 global shock pushed it to 13.9% in 2022 and 14.0% in 2023 on food prices, before rapid tightening brought it down to 4.8% in 2024 and a projected 7.0% in 2025. The National Bank of Rwanda targets price stability with a managed float and has built credibility; Rwanda's inflation performance is among East Africa's best, reflecting both competent policy and the government's administrative capacity.

key_events.event: Global food-fuel crisis pushed inflation to 15.4%, the series high.
Constitutional referendum allowed Kagame to extend his rule; re-elected with 99% (2017).
COVID-19 pushed debt to 66.7% of GDP, the series high; strong rebound followed.
Ukraine war pushed inflation to 14.0%; rapid tightening restored stability.
Kagame re-elected (July 2024) with about 99% amid criticism of political closure.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued 7%+ growth with inflation contained and debt stabilizing near 65% of GDP, the strongest macro outlook in East Africa. Upside comes from services, conferences, and regional integration; downside is political: the development model depends on a closed political system whose succession is unplanned. Uncertainty is moderate on economics but high on politics, which is the long-term risk no macro framework can hedge.
